participantInstructions: This event is presented to the participant team through the team's reading of the 21st Century Skills, the Performance Indicators, and the Case Study Situation. The team will have thirty (30) minutes to review the case and prepare its presentation. The team will then have up to fifteen (15) minutes to present to the judge and respond to the judge's questions. Both members of the participant team must take part in the presentation and in answering the judge's questions. The team will be evaluated on how well the performance indicators listed below are met. All notes and event materials must be turned in to the judge at the conclusion of the event.
situation:
You are the operations director and the client relations manager at MERIDIAN SCREENING GROUP, a two-year-old employment background screening firm operating on its first round of outside funding. The company's managing partner (judge) has asked the two of you to meet with her this afternoon. MERIDIAN verifies criminal records, employment history, and education credentials for corporate clients, and several of its largest accounts are manufacturers that require candidates to be screened for export control compliance before they can access controlled technology. Cash on hand is limited, and losing even one major account would be difficult to absorb.

MERIDIAN was co-founded by the managing partner and a second partner, a former federal background investigator whose name and credentials anchored the company's early marketing. The two never signed a written partnership agreement; they simply split responsibilities, and the departing partner personally managed client relationships through her own contact records. Last month the partners agreed she would leave the business over a disagreement unrelated to any client matter. Because nothing was ever put in writing, the partners never defined who retains rights to her name, her professional biography, or the client relationships she has personally handled.

Every current brochure, the company website, and several active client proposals still feature the departing partner's name, photograph, and investigative credentials, since her background was the credential MERIDIAN sold to corporate clients when it was new. No law and no signed document requires MERIDIAN to remove her name or prevents the firm from continuing to use it; MERIDIAN owns its own promotional materials outright. Several corporate clients, however, signed on specifically because of her personal reputation, and MERIDIAN has never told any of them that she is leaving the firm.

The managing partner (judge) must decide how MERIDIAN represents itself to clients while the departure is being finalized, and how the accounts the departing partner personally managed should be reassigned within the firm's customer relationship system. Federal regulation of background screening leaves MERIDIAN free to keep marketing under her name for as long as it chooses; the harder question is whether doing so, even though every word of it remains technically true today, would leave clients believing she is still personally involved once she is gone.

The managing partner (judge) wants your recommendation on whether MERIDIAN should continue using the departing partner's name and credentials in its current proposals and marketing until a new campaign is ready, or remove every reference to her immediately and reassign her accounts under the remaining team's own credentials. Whichever path you recommend, address what MERIDIAN should tell the affected corporate clients directly, and how the firm can protect the reputation those accounts were built on without misrepresenting who will actually be handling their screening work going forward.

The managing partner (judge) will greet you in her office and ask you to present your recommendation. She will listen to your presentation, ask her questions, and thank you both for your work once the meeting has concluded.
judgeCharacterization: You are the managing partner (judge) at MERIDIAN SCREENING GROUP. Business background is the same as the situation above. You co-founded the firm two years ago with a second partner, a former federal background investigator, but the two of you never signed a written partnership agreement. Last month you agreed she would leave the business, and because nothing was ever put in writing, you and she never defined who keeps the rights to her name, her professional biography, or the client relationships she personally managed. Your marketing materials, your website, and several active proposals still carry her name and credentials, and nothing in law or contract requires you to remove them. Several corporate clients signed on specifically because of her reputation, and none of them yet know she is leaving. You want the participant team's recommendation on whether to keep using her name and credentials until a new campaign is ready, or remove them immediately and reassign her accounts under the remaining team's own credentials, and on what you should tell the affected clients either way.
judgeQuestions: If we keep her name in front of clients a little longer, what happens when they find out she is already gone?
If we take her name down right away and reassign her accounts, what happens the next time one of those clients calls asking for her?
